turns.question: Should a customer-facing reporting API query Snowflake directly or serve precomputed reporting data from Postgres?
turns.shown:
**Short answer:** For most customer-facing reporting APIs, serve precomputed data from Postgres, and keep Snowflake as the place where the data is computed. This is my judgment. Vendor pages and practitioner posts support it, but I found no independent benchmark. Querying Snowflake directly is reasonable in some cases, listed below.

**What the sources say**
- **Concurrency limits:** By default, Snowflake limits concurrent queries to 8 per warehouse [1], controlled by the MAX_CONCURRENCY_LEVEL setting. That figure comes from a third-party blog, and Snowflake describes it as a soft limit. When load exceeds the limit, additional queries queue until resources free up. [2] Snowflake's own guidance is that multi-cluster warehouses add concurrency but don't make individual queries faster [3]. Customer traffic is spiky and unpredictable, so you would be paying for extra clusters to absorb it.
- **Latency:** Snowflake's own guide says standard tables give inconsistent lookup latency. The result cache only helps identical repeated queries, not per-user lookups, and there is no row-level index. [4]
- **Common industry pattern:** One vendor source says a preferred approach is syncing modeled data from the warehouse to a database that the application uses to serve low-latency results [5]. It also says direct warehouse queries can lead to tight coupling to data models [5]. That source is Hightouch, a reverse-ETL vendor, so it has a stake in this pattern.
- **Reliability:** One practitioner source warns that external queries can fail or add unpredictable load to the warehouse [6]. A customer-facing endpoint can therefore affect your internal analytics workloads.

**Snowflake now offers its own serving options**
Snowflake's documentation lists lower-latency serving of precomputed aggregates through an API or a user interface [7] as a hybrid-table use case. Its guide claims double-digit millisecond latency [4] and says this can replace separate serving layers. It also describes Interactive Tables, which are Dynamic Tables optimized for low-latency serving and queried through a specialized Interactive Warehouse [8]. That guide claims sub-100ms analytical queries. These are Snowflake's own claims, and I didn't verify them independently. Hybrid tables also have limits: one experiment found count queries over hybrid tables took significantly longer than on native tables [9]. That post is about 18 months old, and Snowflake has said hybrid tables have since gotten faster.

**When each choice fits**

| Choose Postgres (precomputed) if… | Query Snowflake directly if… |
|---|---|
| You expect many concurrent users or spiky traffic | Traffic is low and internal-ish, such as a few enterprise customers |
| You need predictable, fast responses (for example, under 200 ms) | Seconds-long responses are acceptable |
| Reports are a known set of aggregates, such as per-tenant daily or monthly metrics | Queries are ad hoc or very varied, so precomputing isn't practical |
| You want customer traffic isolated from internal analytics | Data must be near-real-time and a sync lag is unacceptable |
| You want to avoid Snowflake compute cost scaling with customer usage | You want one copy of the data and no sync pipeline |

**Costs of the Postgres route**
- Data is only as fresh as your sync. Decide the acceptable lag first.
- You maintain a pipeline and a second copy of the data.
- Tenant isolation (such as row-level security) has to be handled in Postgres.
- Postgres is not built for very large scans, so precompute at the grain you serve.

**What would change my answer**
- Before deciding, you would need to know your expected queries per second, your latency target, your freshness requirement, the number of distinct report shapes, and data volume.
- If you're already on Snowflake and want to avoid new infrastructure, trial Interactive or hybrid tables against your own workload. I would not rely on the vendor's latency numbers alone.
- A hybrid is common: serve precomputed aggregates from Postgres and fall back to Snowflake for rare drill-downs, with rate limits.

Sources

[2] Snowflake Multi Cluster Warehouses Done Right — https://www.unraveldata.com/resources/snowflake-multi-cluster-warehouse-done-right (search result age: 25 days ago)
[3] Performance — https://www.snowflake.com/en/developers/guides/well-architected-framework-performance/ (search result age: 363 days ago)
